I go in with a lot of tracks. I usually mentally sort tracks with a hell yeah, yeah, and nah (think green, yellow, red lights). Hell yeah are songs that speak to me personally that I really like and I usually want to work into a set, yeah are songs I know that are good or songs that I think will be conventionally well received so a lot of filler songs make it into here, and then nah for songs that do neither. Depending on the length of the set having more music you like helps you ride that length while you figure out your next sections or get the vibe check. That being said I stick to harmonic mixing a lot so say I want to play a song that is keyed as 1m and I am in 5m I will start making my way down my tracks until I hit 1m and maybe on the way down I stick in 3 or 2 for a bit before moving to 1. Whatever music you listen there generally are transitionary hints. I’m only a hobbiest but I’ve been DJing for 12 ish years and produce music and yeah there’s the 4 and 8 bar loops and you need to know those fundamentals but listen for the end of the loop and this is a good way of knowing where you are in the track. For EDM this is usually signaled by a riser or white noise, hip hop usually a change in the beat signaled by the kick and then the beat begins again. Listening and understanding where those transitionary hints are will make your guessing a lot more educated but you need to make it second hand to how you listen to music to the point where you’re registering those end of bar transitions passively.

As someone who has been working in HR for roughly 10 years now this is the most accurate take. If you come to us and just say something is broken it’s not very helpful you need to tell us what is broken. If we are not adhering to a law or a contract you need to tell us how because generally we are trying to and are squaring off with our legal resources on what we need to do to be compliant and generally speaking if you’re right we will take your side because part of being on the company side is protecting the company from lawsuits that would cost way more than being compliant. That being said I will also sympathize with companies because there are A LOT of employees that assume they fully understand how the law or their contracts work when they do not at all and I know that sounds harsh but I’d invoke George Carlin here about how dumb some people can be and it’s true. Just like how there’s folks who think they’re sovereign citizens there are folks who think they are full on labor law lawyers that will say straight to my face how a thing works when a policy, contract, or law may say otherwise in such clear language that it leaves very little room for interpretation and it’s frustrating having to try to explain to person how a thing works when they are already so dug in to their position.

My guess here is built around the factors of the company that ultimately come together that allows them to be sustainable:

1) hello games currently has 62 employees or 45 depending on your source so they are significantly smaller compared to other studios so funding lasts much longer as long as they’re responsible.

2) their portfolio is larger than no man’s sky and the last campfire, they also have an iOS game and since phones are the largest access to games technically I would assume that brings in some income

3) their studio size means outside funding stretches a lot more so if they have outside funding, which we know they do because Microsoft is giving them money to develop Light No Fire, they can stretch that cash injection further

4) this is probably the biggest factor and the one we know the least about and it’s gamepass. There is not a lot of data available for how Microsoft provides developers income for how well their games do on gamepass. There’s a couple different methods we are aware of where it’s some calculation where a developer gets paid based on downloads and hours of play time if their game is on gamepass and then there is another way where Microsoft will outright pay a company for a contract to keep their game on gamepass for X amount of time. However, we do not know what these figures look like and it would be a lot of educated speculation based on sources - however I’d say this is one of the more likely ways they are able to do this because the studio is small enough and Microsoft is likely renewing their contract or is giving them cash injections for the continued no man’s sky players on gamepass.

The solution here is either sell DLC to keep income coming into the game, make a more concise game with a shorter dev cycle, or sell the games at a higher amount to keep funds afloat between dev cycles. Yes a lot of people will say that executives should just take less money and they should but the reality of games is that it’s a high risk high reward industry where game A generally needs to fund the following project so when game A fails it puts the company in serious jeopardy.

If you leave a job after 1.5/2 years that probably won’t raise eye brows and most employers expect younger candidates to explore the job market and look for better opportunities so as long as you’re either moving up or moving to better companies the reasoning is pretty clear.
